newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bars 16 suspected Japanese war criminals.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bars 16 suspected Japanese war criminals.

text.p: The United States has barred as suspected war criminals 16 Japanese who served in the Japanese imperial army during the Second World War, the Justice Department said on Tuesday.

It said the 16 men had been members of units that conducted inhumane and often fatal experiments or had been involved in forcing hundreds of thousands of women to have sexual relations with Japanese army officers and enlisted men.
The 16 Japanese citizens have been placed on the U.S. government's "watchlist" of aliens barred from entering the country, the Justice Department said.
The move marked the first time that individuals who were not involved in European wartime atrocities had been placed on the watchlist under a 1979 law.
That law bars from the United States individuals implicated in acts of persecution committed by Nazi Germany or its wartime allies.

Some of those barred were members of "Unit 731," an infamous Japanese army detachment in Manchuria that conducted experiments on thousands of prisoners of war and civilians, department officials said.

They said the others were suspected of involvment in the Japanese Army's use of forced sex centres. Women and girls from Korea, China, Taiwan, the Philippines, Burma, Malaysia and what is now Indonesia were held captive in the so-called "comfort women stations," they said.
Eli Rosenbaum, head of the department's Nazi-hunting Office of Special Investigations, said more former members of the Japanese armed forces would be barred as the investigation continues.

By taking action against the suspected war criminals, "the U.S. government is demonstrating that it remembers the victims and their suffering and that it wants to deter others from committing such heinous acts," he said in a statement.
More than 60,000 individuals associated with Nazi persecution have been placed on the watchlist since 1979.
